source.title: Spec-Driven Development in Scrum and Kanban: Where the Spec Actually Lives
source.author: Jaroslaw Wasowski

sections.title: Where the spec lives in the cycle
When it works and when it fails

theses.label: Agents don't ask
theses.text: An AI agent builds exactly what the contract says: where a human would ask a follow-up question, the agent confidently builds the wrong thing.
theses.note: The article's opening contrast: the same team runs one sprint from a story and a conversation, and another from a contract that an agent implements.

theses.label: Spec quality is output quality
theses.text: With an agent in the repository, the quality of the spec becomes the quality of the output.
theses.note: A vague prompt turns the sprint into a string of fixes.

theses.label: Frozen or living spec
theses.text: A spec can be frozen, agreed up front and defended by phase gates, or living, maturing inside the sprint as the implementation teaches the team.
theses.note: The frozen variant is Big Design Up Front, and it is what gives SDD its bad name.

theses.label: Agile never banned docs
theses.text: The Agile Manifesto ranks working software above documentation without excluding documentation; agility is the contract's right to change after the build starts.
theses.note: So the common objection that SDD is waterfall in Markdown targets the spec's presence instead of its being frozen.

theses.label: The tension: frozen vs living
theses.text: The real tension is between a frozen spec and a living one, not between fast delivery and writing specs, and only the frozen spec deserves the waterfall charge.

theses.label: AI: faster greenfield, slower legacy
theses.text: AI assistance sped up a greenfield task in a controlled study but slowed experienced developers down on a mature repository with millions of lines of code.
theses.note: Different conditions, different results: the author reads them as two ends of the same axis.

theses.label: The spec closes the gaps
theses.text: On mature code, gaps a human would question turn into wrong implementations, so the spec is the place to close them before the agent starts building.

theses.label: Three rungs of SDD
theses.text: SDD comes in three levels: spec-first, spec-anchored and spec-as-source, and each higher rung raises the maintenance cost and the coupling between spec and code.
theses.note: The classification is by Birgitta Böckeler of Thoughtworks. Spec-first: the spec leads, the code is maintained. Spec-anchored: the spec is versioned and evolves with the code. Spec-as-source: the spec is the source of truth, the code is generated and disposable.

theses.label: "Spec" is a blurry word
theses.text: "Spec" can mean anything from an elaborate prompt to dozens of Markdown files, so any SDD statistic is meaningless without its level.
theses.note: Conflating levels is, in the author's words, the costliest mistake in the whole topic.

theses.label: Pick the lowest rung that fits
theses.text: Most work should stay at spec-first, shared contracts such as public APIs justify spec-anchored, and spec-as-source belongs to experiments and safety-critical systems.
theses.note: The one antipattern is paying for a higher rung while the problem sits on a lower one, such as a simple bug that spawns several stories and a dozen acceptance criteria.

theses.label: The spec lives in the sprint
theses.text: The backlog should stay at the level of goal and intent, and the contract should be developed inside the sprint, as part of doing the work.
theses.note: The author credits Yuval Yeret with this placement. A finished contract in the backlog signals a spec at the wrong level of abstraction.

theses.label: The spec feeds the DoR
theses.text: A spec already supplies what a Definition of Ready asks for: acceptance criteria, scope boundaries and edge cases.

theses.label: A DoR can become a gate
theses.text: A Definition of Ready can turn into a gatekeeper that blocks the iteration and drifts back toward waterfall.
theses.note: This is Mike Cohn's warning, quoted in the article.

theses.label: Scrum: DoR as agreement
theses.text: In Scrum the spec belongs in the Definition of Ready, treated as the team's agreement on entry quality rather than a phase gate.

theses.label: Kanban: the commitment point
theses.text: In Kanban the commitment point takes the role of the Definition of Ready, and WIP limits in Upstream Kanban keep specs from going stale before anyone builds them.
theses.note: A task crosses the commitment point only when it is ready to pull: there is clarity about what to build.

theses.label: Fitted specs paid off
theses.text: Where the spec matched the scale of the problem, quality improved in three different contexts.
theses.note: A Scrum quasi-experiment with an architectural spec (sMBSAP, Colorado State, 2023): velocity up about 19%, defect density down about 31%. A semiconductor product line: about half the defects despite higher complexity. A global bank: firefighting dropped from over a third of developer time to single digits after nine months of behavior-driven specs.

theses.label: Mismatched specs failed
theses.text: Where the spec level didn't fit, or SDD was imposed as a mandate, it slowed teams down and turned them against it.
theses.note: A practitioner measured roughly a tenfold slowdown with a rigid SDD workflow on a small CRUD feature, with more Markdown than code to review. Another rollout, imposed top-down, met a petition of more than a thousand engineers; the author notes that some details are unverified.

theses.label: Fit decides, not presence
theses.text: What decides the outcome is fitting the spec level to the context, not the mere presence of a spec.

theses.label: Perception isn't measurement
theses.text: Developers who expected AI to speed them up by about 24% were measured to be about 19% slower on a mature repository.
theses.note: METR, 2025: sixteen developers, wide confidence interval. The author calls the gap between perception and metrics the real opponent.

theses.label: Roll it out as an experiment
theses.text: SDD should be rolled out as an experiment that tracks cycle time, rework rate and the ratio of code to Markdown, and the batch size should shrink when rework or spec files grow faster than code.

theses.label: One owner, few invariants
theses.text: A living spec needs a single owner, a version history and only a small set of invariant rules, or spec drift comes back.
theses.note: Too many fixed constraints don't add order; they add places for contradictions to hide.

theses.label: Living, fitted, measured
theses.text: SDD strengthens Agile when the spec is living: developed inside the sprint, or before the commitment point in Kanban, as an agreement rather than a gate, at the level the problem needs, and judged by measurement rather than by feel.
theses.note: The article's answer to its opening question: the faster sprint was the one where the spec lived inside the sprint at the right level.

issues.explanation: The mandate failure is about how SDD was introduced, not about the level of the spec, yet it's taken as evidence that fitting the level decides the outcome.
issues.quote: Still, the conclusion is clear: what decides the outcome is fitting the level to the context, not the mere presence of a spec.

issues.explanation: The article never says which level of spec the three success cases used: the fit is read off the good outcome, so the cases assume the fit they're meant to show.
issues.quote: Three different contexts, one direction: when the spec matched the scale of the problem, quality went up.

issues.explanation: SDD is defined as an AI agent building from a contract, but none of the three success cases involves an agent: they show that specs helped, not that SDD with agents does.
issues.quote: In a quasi-experiment comparing Scrum with a version enriched by an architectural spec (sMBSAP, Colorado State, 2023)

issues.explanation: "Level" is a rung of the ladder in 8, 10 and 18, but a level of abstraction (goal or finished contract) in 11; the sentence treats a finished contract in the backlog as a lower rung.
issues.quote: Placing a finished, complete contract in the backlog is a signal that the spec sits at the wrong level of abstraction, one rung too low relative to the intent.

issues.explanation: Each is presented as the one thing that decides: frozen versus living in 5, fitting the level in 18. Both can hold only if neither is the single deciding factor the article calls it.
issues.quote: The rest of this article is just the unpacking of that one distinction.

issues.explanation: The opening compares a sprint that starts from a story with one that starts from a contract; the summary answers by comparing a living contract with a frozen one, a pair the opening never set up.
issues.quote: The one that delivered faster was the one where the spec lived inside the sprint at the right level — not the one that got a finished, frozen contract handed down from the backlog.

senses.definition: A precise contract written before the code, from which an AI agent builds the implementation.
Any practice that writes a spec before the code, with or without an agent.
A rung of Böckeler's ladder: spec-first, spec-anchored or spec-as-source.
A level of abstraction: goal and intent, or a finished contract.
A contract that matures inside the sprint as the implementation teaches the team.
A design agreed up front and defended against change by phase gates.
The criteria a task must meet before it enters the sprint.
In Kanban, the moment a task stops being optional and becomes a commitment to deliver.
The gap between the spec and the code once there are more documents than the team can maintain.

reconstructed.reason: A general claim about agents, backed only by the author's description; no study or case is cited.
Defines the two kinds of spec the article compares.
Checkable in the Manifesto itself, whose authors say there is value in the items on the right.
Two studies that differ in task, tool and developers, so the contrast isn't controlled; the second (METR, 2025) had sixteen developers.

condition.text: Nothing but gaps no one questioned explains the slowdown on mature code.
condition.reason: questionable cause: the study doesn't say why the developers were slower

reconstructed.reason: A named, checkable classification by Birgitta Böckeler of Thoughtworks.
Shown by the ladder itself: one word covers three levels with different costs.

condition.text: No other choice of level fits the costs of the three levels better.
condition.reason: each level's cost is weighed against where it pays off

condition.text: Developing the contract inside the sprint is the best way to keep the spec living.
condition.reason: the alternative, a finished contract in the backlog, is shown to freeze it

reconstructed.reason: Common knowledge: acceptance criteria, scope boundaries and edge cases are what both contain.
Mike Cohn's warning, quoted; he writes on this exact point.

condition.text: Treating the DoR as an agreement is the best way to use the spec without a gate.
Kanban's commitment point is like Scrum's DoR in the respect that matters: it's where a task must be ready to build.
condition.reason: the article states the shared role: a task crosses it only when it's ready to pull

reconstructed.label:
Specs preceded
better quality
reconstructed.text: In three different contexts, quality improved after a team introduced a spec.
reconstructed.note: A Scrum quasi-experiment with an architectural spec (sMBSAP, Colorado State, 2023): velocity up about 19%, defect density down about 31%. A semiconductor product line: about half the defects despite higher complexity. A global bank: firefighting dropped from over a third of developer time to single digits after nine months of behavior-driven specs.
reconstructed.reason: Three single cases: one quasi-experiment on a single project, one product line, and one bank where the drop came after nine months of specs, which shows sequence, not cause.

reconstructed.label:
Those specs
fitted
reconstructed.text: In those three contexts, the spec matched the scale of the problem.
reconstructed.reason: The article never says which level of spec each case used; the fit is read off the good outcome.

reconstructed.label:
Rigid SDD
slowed a CRUD
reconstructed.text: A rigid SDD workflow on a small CRUD feature slowed a practitioner down roughly tenfold.
reconstructed.note: The tool generated more Markdown than code, and all of it had to be reviewed: spec drift in its early stage.
reconstructed.reason: One practitioner's experiment on one feature; the source isn't named.

reconstructed.label:
A mandate
backfired
reconstructed.text: SDD imposed top-down as a mandate turned the organization against it.
reconstructed.note: A petition of more than a thousand engineers, with metric-gaming in the background.
reconstructed.reason: The author's own hedge: some details of the story are unverified.

condition.text: Nothing but the fit of the spec level explains why some rollouts paid off and others failed.
condition.reason: the fit is judged after the fact, and other differences between the cases aren't ruled out

reconstructed.reason: A named, checkable study (METR, 2025), with its limits stated: sixteen developers, wide confidence interval.

condition.text: An experiment with tracked metrics is the best way to roll out SDD.
condition.reason: the measured gap between perception and speed calls for metrics, and the alternative, a mandate, failed

condition.text: A single owner, a version history and few invariants are what keep spec drift away.
condition.reason: drift appeared exactly where specs multiplied without an owner
